problem: Target-driven visual navigation policies learned by imitation or RL regress actions directly from (observation, target) pairs, yet the action distribution is multi-modal. This hurts data efficiency and cross-scene/cross-target generalization, and the policies also collide and struggle to decide when to stop.
motivation: Mapless target-driven navigation without odometry or GPS needs policies that generalize to unseen scenes and new target images. Multiple valid actions per state make direct action regression high-variance, and the single stop action is heavily under-represented in trajectories. The authors move the multi-modality into a generative next-observation step and add auxiliary modules for safety and termination.
key_idea: Before choosing an action, imagine the next expected observation (NEO) with a conditional variational generative module trained from expert demonstrations, then predict the action from the current and imagined observations. This is aided by premature collision prediction and a separate target-checking module for stopping.
insight: Moving the multi-modality into NEO generation makes the observation-to-action mapping a surjection, which improves generalization. Removing the variational generative module (Ours-NoVG) drops unseen-scene SR from 28.7 to 22.6, and removing target checking (Ours-NoTC) drops it to 19.8. Removing collision prediction (Ours-NoCP) raises collisions from 48.1 to 56.2, and Ours also beats NeoNav, which lacks the added modules and feature-space dynamics (28.7 vs 17.5 SR). Depth input beats RGB (28.7 vs 21.3 SR), and RGB+depth is worse than depth alone.
method: Variational generative module: an ELBO-trained model with q(z|x_t,g) and prior p(z|x_t,a_t) (mixture-of-posteriors prior conditioned on the GT action) and decoder p(x_{t+1}|z); loss is reconstruction (alpha=0.01) plus KL (beta=0.0001), so multi-modality is absorbed into NEO generation.
Predictive control: a controller q(a_t|x_t, x_{t+1}, a_{t-1}) trained with cross-entropy (gamma=1) predicts the action from the current view, the generated NEO and the previous action.

Feature-space dynamics: a shared lightweight CNN (spectral-norm conv, LeakyReLU, 64x64 input to 512-D) encodes observations, and NEO reconstruction is done in feature space, which is cheaper to train than VGG16 or ResNet50 at similar accuracy.

Premature collision prediction (CPM): an MLP on the fused four-view features predicts multi-label collision probability for all 7 actions, with weight zeta=0.4, giving a safety-oriented auxiliary signal to the shared CNN.

Target checking (TCM): a binary stop/move classifier on the fused four-view feature plus the target feature, with weight eta=0.4. About 1/|A| of training tasks start at the target to counter class imbalance, replacing the stop action in the policy.

Setup: four-camera panoramic observation (0/90/180/270 degrees) and discrete actions (move forward/back/left/right 0.5 m, rotate ±30°, stop). Trained on Dijkstra expert trajectories; total loss L = L_pi + 0.4 L_cp + 0.4 L_tc.

setting.backbone: Custom small CNN (spectral norm) + variational generative module + MLP heads, trained from scratch
setting.training_data: Dijkstra expert trajectories from the Active Vision Dataset (15 target views per training scene by default; 120/240/360 target views in a scaling study), AI2-THOR kitchens, and a self-collected TurtleBot dataset from three office scenes (AVD-pretrained model transferred)
setting.observation: four-view panoramic RGB or depth (64x64 each); the target is an image; no odometry or GPS
setting.action_space: discrete: move forward/back/left/right (0.5 m), rotate cw/ccw 30°, stop; max 100 steps
setting.simulator: Active Vision Dataset (real-captured scenes, discrete positions) and AI2-THOR; real TurtleBot2
setting.privileged: none at test time (GT shortest-path expert trajectories used only for training)

results: On AVD unseen environments, the method reaches 28.7 SR / 8.8 SPL with depth, against 17.5 / 4.4 for its predecessor NeoNav, with about 16.3% fewer collisions. It also beats GSP (23.4 SR at 120 views) and TD-A3C-IL (20.7). On AI2-THOR unseen scenes it gets 47.32/22.09 SR/SPL versus 41.09/7.20 for LSTM-A3C-KG-A, and on a real TurtleBot it gets 62% SR on training scenes and 30% on unseen scenes, ahead of GSP (58%/22%).
limitations: Absolute success rates in unseen scenes are low (about 29% SR on AVD, 30% on the real robot), and there is a large seen/unseen gap.
Discrete action commands produce jerky, oscillatory robot motion, and the agent gets stuck when the start view has no overlap with the target.
There is no attention over relevant image regions, the auxiliary loss weights are hand-tuned, and real-world evaluation is small (50 tasks per setting).
